title: Unrestricted arithmetic lower bounds for the discrete Fourier transform
formal: Let \(S(n)\) be the minimum size of a complex arithmetic straight-line program that computes all n coordinates of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) exactly, in the model below. Do constants \(c>0\) and N exist such that \(S(n)\ge c n \log _{2}n\) for every power of two \(n\ge N\), with no bound on the magnitudes of the constants used in the program?
why: Tests whether the central FFT upper bound is inherently necessary in unrestricted arithmetic computation.

progress.text: The circuit reference recalls Morgenstern’s bounded-coefficient DFT lower bound and gives related bounded-coefficient bilinear lower bounds. Its model section distinguishes the unrestricted arithmetic and linear formulations.
Theorem 2.1 proves an n log n lower bound for normalized Fourier computation in a two-coordinate unitary model with n storage locations.
The revised paraunitary paper and its journal version study speedup versus algebraic conditioning, retaining restrictions beyond this card’s model.
The SODA source proves division lower bounds for integer-point Toom-Cook interpolation in specified cost models, not the unrestricted DFT target.

references.title: Wikipedia: Fast Fourier transform
references.locator: Discovery source; retrieved 2026-09-11. Evidence locator: lower bounds

definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) set \(\omega _{n}=\exp (- 2\pi i/n)\), and define \(DFT_{n}(x)_{j}=\sum_{k=0}^{n- 1}\omega _{n}^{jk}x_{k}\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,n- 1\) and \(x\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every \(c>0\) and every threshold N there is a power of two \(n\ge N\) and a program of size less than \(c n \log _{2}n\). A family using \(o(n \log  n)\) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.

context_blocks.title: A fast transform reuses intermediate values
context_blocks.text: For four inputs, form \(a=x_{0}+x_{2}, b=x_{1}+x_{3}, c=x_{0}- x_{2}\) and \(d=x_{1}- x_{3}\). The four Fourier outputs are \(a+b, c- id, a- b\) and \(c+id\). Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

context_blocks.title: Normalization should not decide this question
context_blocks.text: Dividing all outputs by \(\sqrt{n}\) gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

context_blocks.title: What the classical lower bound assumes
context_blocks.text: Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is \(n^{n/2}\), whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

context_blocks.title: Unitary and well-conditioned models
context_blocks.text: Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

context_blocks.title: Related tasks use different cost measures
context_blocks.text: The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.

sentences: Must the discrete Fourier transform take order n log n exact arithmetic operations when constants are unrestricted?
The target covers every sufficiently large power-of-two input length and all straight-line programs in the stated model.
The FFT achieves this cost by sharing intermediate computations.
Known matching lower bounds impose coefficient, gate, storage or conditioning restrictions.
Normalization, bit precision and quantum state transformations require care because their computational models differ.
